outline.description: Sets out the executive actions that triggered the litigation, the parties’ claims, the district court’s preliminary injunctions, and the Ninth Circuit’s evolving stay orders leading to this interlocutory order.
subtopics: Executive Order 14163 (Jan. 20, 2025): suspension of refugee entry under 8 U.S.C. §§ 1182(f), 1185(a)
Executive Order 14169 (Jan. 24, 2025): suspension of USRAP-related funding as part of foreign aid reevaluation
Plaintiffs: admitted refugees, refugees approved but abroad, and three resettlement organizations with State Department cooperative agreements

District court actions: Feb. 25 oral PI enjoining E.O. 14163 §§ 3(a)–(c), 4; Feb. 28 written PI specifying funding suspension prohibited; Mar. 24 PI ordering reinstatement of terminated cooperative agreements

Government appeals (Feb. 28 and Mar. 25 notices) and motions panel’s Mar. 25 partial stay with carveout for individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before Jan. 20, 2025; Apr. 21 and May 9 clarifications
Post-briefing developments: July 14 enforcement framework and magistrate appointment; July 17 emergency motion; July 18 administrative stay; Sept. 3 expedited oral argument

Current order: vacates prior stays (Mar. 25 and amendments; July 18), issues new stay pending appeal with an exception for statutorily required services, and denies the July 17 emergency motion as moot

outline.chapter_title: Legal Questions and Governing Law for a Stay Pending Appeal
outline.description: Frames the central issues and the legal standards controlling interim relief, including the scope of presidential authority over entry and the statutory and APA constraints on defunding refugee services.
subtopics: Stay standard under Nken v. Holder: likelihood of success, irreparable injury, injury to others, and public interest; first two factors are most critical
Presidential power to suspend entry: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) and deference principles from Trump v. Hawaii
Refugee Act framework: 8 U.S.C. § 1522 (resettlement services), § 1523 (reporting), and implementing regulations at 45 C.F.R. §§ 400.200 et seq.
APA challenges to defunding and termination of cooperative agreements: contrary-to-law and related theories
Appropriations context: FY 2025 migration and refugee assistance funding (with subsequent rescission) and its relevance to § 1522’s “to the extent of available appropriations” language
Mechanisms for delivering services: contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements with nonprofit agencies under § 1522(b)(1)(A)(ii)

outline.chapter_title: Interim Merits Assessment: Authority to Suspend Refugee Admissions
outline.description: Explains the court’s conclusion that the government is likely to succeed in defending the entry suspension under § 1182(f), and how that drives the stay analysis for that aspect of the case.
subtopics: Textual breadth of § 1182(f): suspension of entry of any class of aliens based on presidential detriment finding
Limits on judicial review: no “searching inquiry” into the President’s justifications per Trump v. Hawaii
Application to E.O. 14163: the President made the requisite detriment finding; the order fits § 1182(f)’s scope
Balancing the Nken factors: domestic and foreign policy interests, irreparable harm to the government, and public interest favor a stay of the injunction against the entry suspension

outline.chapter_title: Interim Merits Assessment: Statutory Duties to Provide Post-Admission Services
outline.description: Details why the court finds the government not likely to prevail on at least one APA challenge tied to statutory obligations under § 1522, and how that leads to a targeted exception to the stay.
subtopics: Statutory mandates identified by the panel: § 1522(a)(1)(A) (Director “shall,” to the extent of available appropriations, ensure core support services); § 1522(d)(2)(B) (Director “shall assume” legal/financial responsibility for unaccompanied minors, if necessary); § 1522(e)(7)(A) (Secretary “shall develop and implement” support projects for recent arrivals)
Implementing regulations: 45 C.F.R. §§ 400.200 et seq. describing federally funded refugee services
Appropriations context: Congress funded migration and refugee assistance for FY 2025 (with partial rescission), supporting the availability predicate
Delivery mechanism: historical reliance on cooperative agreements with resettlement organizations under § 1522(b)(1)(A)(ii)
Record facts: termination of cooperative agreements on Feb. 26, 2025; government’s RFP representation (Mar. 10) and subsequent uncertainty about progress at oral argument
Targeted relief: direction to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide usual and customary § 1522 reception and placement services to already-admitted refugees pending appeal

outline.chapter_title: Operative Order: What Is Stayed and What Must Proceed
outline.description: Precisely delineates the court’s directives, including what aspects of the district court’s injunctions are stayed and the carveout requiring service provision for admitted refugees.
subtopics: Vacatur of prior appellate stays: administrative stay (July 18) and earlier stay (Mar. 25) as amended (Apr. 21, May 9)
Global stay of district court’s Feb. 28 and Mar. 24 preliminary injunctions, except for the services-related carveout

Carveout and mandate: government must reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide reception and placement services under § 1522 to refugees already admitted to the United States, including usual/customary services
Emergency motion (July 17) denied as moot
Case submitted after expedited argument; full merits opinion to follow

outline.chapter_title: Separate Opinion: The § 1522 Dispute and Its Implications
outline.description: Summarizes Judge Lee’s partial concurrence/dissent, highlighting the statutory-interpretation divide over whether § 1522 mandates or merely authorizes services and the practical consequences for interim relief.
subtopics: Agreement with majority: stay of injunction as to the President’s entry suspension under § 1182(f)
Core disagreement: § 1522 as permissive authorization, not a mandate; emphasis on title (“Authorization”), repeated “is authorized” phrasing in § 1522(b)–(e)
Reading of § 1522(a): “shall” conditions apply only if the executive chooses to fund assistance under § 1522(b)–(e); not an independent spending mandate
Treatment of § 1522(d)(2)(B) and § 1522(e)(7)(A): qualified obligations (“if necessary,” “as needed”) preserving executive discretion
Remedial consequence: would fully stay the district court’s injunctions without requiring reinstatement of cooperative agreements or services during the appeal

Issues to watch for in the forthcoming opinion: definitive construction of § 1522; APA ‘contrary to law’ versus discretion; scope of judicial authority to compel contractual mechanisms to satisfy statutory duties; harmonization of § 1182(f) entry power with post-admission statutory obligations
